strengths: Addresses an important and timely NLP security problem: indirect prompt injection in third-party context processed by LLMs.

Proposes a novel intervention at the Key-Value cache level, identifying and suppressing feature dimensions associated with instruction-following rather than modifying prompts or adding per-response LLM calls after calibration.
The method is practically appealing because it is compatible with context caching and existing prompt-level defenses and incurs no obvious additional generation cost once the mask has been computed.

Empirical results on LLaMA3-8B and Mistral-7B across SQuAD, HotpotQA, and WildChat show substantial reductions in attack success rate while generally preserving clean-response F1 or LLM-judge quality.
Includes useful ablations on pruning ratio, the number of triggering tokens k, masking strength alpha, layer-wise neuron distribution, and transfer between text- and code-based attacks.

The triggering-effect observation—that only the first few response tokens are needed to distinguish clean versus poisoned behavior—is interesting and helps make the attribution procedure sample-efficient.
weaknesses: The claimed DPO upper-bound derivation is not fully convincing. The assumptions that the reference model makes the margin positive, the Jensen step, the omission of log-sigmoid and beta, and the entropy/support decompositions around Equations 29–32 require clarification or correction; Equation (20) also appears to contain a typo.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The paper should state clearly whether the neuron mask is global per model, per dataset, or per prompt; how the eight calibration prompts are selected; whether masks are shared across all test prompts; and exactly how and where the KV features are masked.

The claim of no extra test-time computation needs qualification: producing the mask requires offline clean/poisoned sampling and gradient computation. The associated wall-clock, memory, and gradient overhead are not reported.

Security evaluation is largely limited to static, non-adaptive injections. There is no evaluation against an adaptive attacker who knows the pruning mask and uses obfuscated, multilingual, distributed, multi-turn, or otherwise novel payloads.

The experimental scope is relatively narrow: two open 7B/8B-scale models, three tasks, about 400 prompts per setting, and mainly one injection suite. Larger models, API-like constrained settings, and broader out-of-domain benchmarks would strengthen the claims.

The baselines are mostly simple prompt-engineering methods. Additional controls such as random pruning, pruning from clean-only gradients, other activation-editing defenses, or selected training-based defenses would better isolate the value of the proposed attribution.

The definition and detection of Attack Success Rate are not sufficiently explained, especially for open-ended WildChat responses evaluated with an LLM judge. Judge prompts, reliability checks, and annotation criteria should be included.
Notation and writing require polish, including several typos such as ‘triggerring’, ‘greegy’, ‘experiemnt’, ‘correspondinggly’, and ‘undersdanding’.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important security problem for deployed LLMs: indirect prompt injection through untrusted context.
The proposed intervention is practically attractive: it leaves the prompt unchanged, adds no per-response LLM calls, and prunes only a small fraction of KV-cache features.

The reported results show a promising security–utility trade-off on several settings, for example reducing Llama3-8B ASR on SQuAD from 27.86 to 7.44 while maintaining clean F1 around 28.7, and on HotpotQA from 69.01 to 15.23 while maintaining clean F1 around 16.2.
The evaluation includes two widely used open models, three datasets, injection at different context positions, and several simple no-additional-call baselines.
Ablations over pruning ratio, masking strength alpha, number of triggering tokens, layer distribution, and text/code transfer provide some initial insight into the method.
weaknesses: The deployment and threat model is unclear. It is not evident whether the mask is learned once from eight attacked prompts and reused globally, or computed for each new context. The former raises adaptive-attack concerns, while the latter would conflict with the claim of no extra test-time computation.

The security evaluation is too narrow. It primarily uses one attack construction and does not test adaptive attackers, obfuscated injections, multi-turn attacks, tool-use scenarios, varied instruction styles, or attacks specifically designed to bypass the pruned features.

The central claim that the model is forced to treat context as 'pure data' is overstated. Behavioral ASR reductions do not establish this causal interpretation; the attributed features may instead capture response content, answer style, or task-specific tokens.

The attribution loss is derived from a DPO upper bound, but the derivation makes strong assumptions about the reference model and leaves the role of beta, sigmoid, constants, and signs unclear. Lemma 1 only examines limiting cases and does not establish a generally reliable relationship between the two objectives.

Equation (2) defines attack success using membership in the support of a response distribution, which is not operational because softmax LMs assign nonzero probability to almost all sequences. A concrete attack-success classifier or judging protocol is needed.

The use of first-token or first-few-token attribution is questionable. Figure 7 shows that these tokens are often generic response starters such as 'The', 'According', or 'Based', so the method may be selecting style-related features rather than neurons encoding the data/instruction boundary.

Important ablation baselines are missing, including random pruning, activation-magnitude pruning, standard gradient or integrated-gradient attribution, a sham loss, and sensitivity to the number N of identification samples. Consequently, neither the attribution quality nor the claimed eight-sample efficiency is convincingly demonstrated.

Utility is evaluated only with same-task F1 and a GPT-based summary score. Pruning instruction-associated features could harm general instruction following, reasoning, or refusals; broader benchmarks such as instruction-following and capability evaluations are necessary.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper does not provide code, the eight identification prompts, full attack templates, ASR annotation details, a precise algorithm, or a complete description of whether keys, values, or both are masked and how the mask persists during generation.
Some reported utility drops are non-trivial, such as Mistral-7B clean SQuAD F1 falling from 28.28 to 24.46, so the blanket statement that response quality is not compromised is too strong.

The related-work discussion omits relevant activation-engineering, representation-pruning, circuit-breaking, and backdoor-removal approaches, making the novelty relative to existing neural feature-editing defenses difficult to assess.
Presentation quality needs improvement: there are numerous typos and inconsistent notations, and the term 'neuron' is used ambiguously for scalar dimensions in the key/value feature tensor.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely NLP security problem: indirect prompt injection in retrieved or third-party context. The idea of intervening directly on the context Key-Value cache, rather than rewriting prompts or adding test-time LLM calls, is novel and practically appealing.

The CachePrune pipeline is conceptually clear: identify KV-cache dimensions associated with poisoned versus clean responses, aggregate scores over time, restrict pruning to a carefully defined neuron subset, and mask only a small fraction of dimensions. The DPO-inspired attribution and triggering-effect motivation provide a useful mechanistic perspective.

The main empirical results are strong across two open model families, Llama3-8B and Mistral-7B, and three settings: SQuAD, HotpotQA, and WildChat. CachePrune substantially lowers attack success rates while largely preserving clean-response F1 and WildChat response quality.

The paper includes useful ablations on the number of triggering tokens k, masking strength alpha, pruning percentage p, layer-wise neuron distribution, and transfer between code- and text-based attacks. These analyses support the design choices and make the contribution more interpretable.

After one-time calibration with eight samples and a 0.5% neuron mask, the method introduces no additional LLM calls for individual responses and is complementary to prompt-based or workflow-based defenses. This efficiency is a meaningful advantage over many existing mitigations.
weaknesses: I rate the paper as borderline conference rather than a clear main-conference accept because the empirical threat model and theoretical derivation are not yet fully convincing. The core results are promising, but the broader claim that CachePrune reliably enforces a data-versus-instruction boundary needs stronger validation.

The deployment assumptions are under-emphasized. CachePrune requires white-box model access, differentiable access to KV-cache activations, knowledge of context boundaries, and a small calibration set containing comparable attacks. The no-extra-test-time-calls claim holds only after this setup, and the one-time gradient, memory, latency, and mask-construction costs are not reported.

Evaluation breadth is limited. The experiments cover only two similarly sized decoder-only models and are dominated by QA-style injections, with one WildChat setting. There are no agent/tool-use, long-context, multi-turn, instruction-following, or modern agent-injection benchmarks. It is also unclear how broadly a model- or dataset-specific mask transfers to new tasks and attack distributions.

The baselines are mostly lightweight prompt-engineering methods. Several cited training-based or stronger test-time defenses are not compared, even under a clearly labeled different-cost setting. More statistical information, such as significance tests or confidence intervals over evaluation prompts, would also strengthen the conclusions.

No adaptive attack is evaluated. A security-aware attacker could rephrase, obfuscate, distribute, or relocate malicious instructions to avoid the identified neurons. Demonstrating robustness to adaptive attacks is especially important for a defense paper and is necessary to establish that the method does not merely suppress patterns in the benchmark attacks.

The theoretical argument has technical issues. In Appendix A, equation (20) appears to use the wrong inequality, the proof repeatedly cites (19) when it likely means (20), and the reference-model assumptions are not clearly operationalized in the experiments. The limiting argument in Lemma 1 also does not adequately control the exponential response-support size, so the attribution loss should be presented more explicitly as a well-motivated approximation.

Reproducibility could be improved. The paper should detail how poisoned responses and ASR are automatically determined, provide exact calibration/test splits and attack templates, specify random seeds and implementation details for KV-cache masking, and state whether code and masks will be released. There are also several notation and typographical errors, including misspellings such as 'triggerring,' 'greegy,' and 'correspondinggly.'

strengths: The paper proposes a novel and practical KV-cache-level defense: it identifies dimensions that make the model treat contextual data as instructions and prunes those dimensions only for the context span. After a one-time calibration stage, it requires no prompt rewriting, no additional test-time LLM calls, and is compatible with context caching.

The method is technically coherent and well decomposed into preferential attribution scoring, gradient-by-activation neuron scores, temporal aggregation, selective thresholding, and intervention. The triggering-effect observation also gives a plausible sample-efficiency mechanism.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the core claim: three open LLMs, SQuAD, HotpotQA, and WildChat, multiple attack positions and attack families, clean and attacked response-quality metrics, repeated trials with standard deviations, prune-ratio curves, layer analyses, text/code transfer, cross-attack mask transfer, and adaptive attacks.

CachePrune consistently achieves large reductions in attack success rate relative to vanilla and prompt-formatting defenses while generally preserving clean F1, ROUGE, BERTScore, or GPT-judge quality. The comparison with Encode_Base64 usefully shows that some low-ASR baselines obtain security by substantially damaging utility.
The appendices strengthen reproducibility by describing attack templates, positive/negative sampling, metrics, hyperparameters, ablations, adaptive-attack details, and evaluation code snippets.
weaknesses: The deployment assumptions are narrower than some of the paper's broader claims. The method requires known context/user boundaries and offline clean-versus-poisoned examples. It is not fully clear how masks are reused across models, tasks, and datasets, and cross-dataset generalization is not convincingly isolated.

The evidence for "no compromise in response quality" is limited to the evaluated tasks. Because the mask prunes global KV dimensions, it could affect unrelated instruction following, reasoning, safety behavior, or general knowledge. Broad benchmarks such as MMLU, MT-Bench, or general instruction-following suites are needed to support a more general utility claim.

The baselines are mostly prompt-formatting methods. Stronger detectors that refuse suspicious inputs, robust-finetuning approaches, or existing activation/neuron-editing defenses would better establish CachePrune's comparative advantage, even if they have different computational costs.

The adaptive-attack evaluation is promising but limited in budget and diversity: it uses a small number of calibration prompts, relatively few GCG steps, and one attack parameterization. Stronger untargeted attacks, larger token/step budgets, and attacks that jointly try to evade the learned threshold would increase confidence.

The theoretical justification is not fully rigorous as written. Theorem 1 and Lemma 1 depend on strong reference-model assumptions, fixed finite response supports, and asymptotic probability regimes; the finite-sample connection between the DPO objective and the simplified probability-difference loss remains heuristic. There also appear to be typographical errors in the reference-model inequalities used in the proof.

Some reproducibility and evaluation details remain underspecified, including the exact mask-fitting pipeline per dataset, random-seed handling, stability of masks derived from only eight examples, and the precise automatic criteria or judge prompts used to label attack success and partial compliance. The manuscript also contains numerous notation and spelling errors that should be corrected.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely NLP security problem: defending LLMs against indirect prompt injection without changing the visible prompt format.

Proposes a reasonably novel activation-level intervention that identifies and masks KV-cache neurons associated with poisoned instruction-following behavior, rather than relying solely on prompt templates or refusal detectors.
The method is sample-efficient, using only eight calibration examples in the main setting, and a learned mask can be reused across prompts; it is also conceptually compatible with context/KV caching.

Experiments cover three modern open models, two question-answering datasets, and a dialogue-summarization scenario, with additional transfer, adaptive-attack, layer, prune-ratio, trigger-token, and regularization ablations.
The main results consistently show lower attack-success rates while preserving clean-task F1, with ROUGE and BERTScore providing some corroboration that response quality is not severely degraded.
The paper includes substantial appendix material on hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, attack templates, sampling, and adaptive attacks, which aids understanding of the approach.
weaknesses: The central claim that pruning makes the model treat context 'purely as data' is stronger than the evidence supports. The experiments demonstrate reduced attack success on tested benchmarks, but do not establish a general mechanism for separating data and instructions.

The method is not overhead-free or universally deployable: it requires offline contrastive response generation, backpropagation through the model, identification of context boundaries, and access to internal KV caches. These requirements should be stated more prominently, especially because ordinary API users cannot perform such pruning.

The attribution targets are approximate counterfactuals obtained by removing or inserting trigger phrases and using greedy responses. Their validity as proxies for true clean versus poisoned responses is not systematically evaluated, and gradient-times-activation attribution can be unstable without a stronger baseline or integrated-gradient justification.

The DPO-based theoretical motivation is idealized and does not convincingly validate the practical attribution procedure. In particular, the reference-model assumptions are strong, several asymptotic quantities are unrealistic, and there are notation and likely typographical issues in the proof, including Equations (20)–(21).

Generalization remains uncertain. The mask is learned from a very small number of examples drawn from similar attack distributions, and evaluation is limited to English QA/summarization-style tasks. Performance on real RAG, tool-use, agent workflows, multilingual attacks, or contexts containing legitimate instructions is not demonstrated.

The baseline comparison is relatively narrow. The main baselines are simple prompt-engineering methods; stronger structured-prompting, detection, fine-tuning, or activation-editing defenses are not directly compared. The adaptive attack is also valuable but may not be fully optimized against the hard pruning mask, and its exact threat model and optimization procedure need clarification.

The ASR definition and annotation procedure are under-specified in the main paper, particularly how a response is classified as poisoned, how partial compliance is handled, and how reliable the automatic or LLM-based judgments are. The WildChat evaluation relies heavily on GPT scoring without reported inter-rater agreement or human validation.

Reproducibility would benefit from an explicit code release and clearer disclosure of whether one mask is trained per model, dataset, or attack family; how the eight calibration prompts are sampled; how the threshold unit p corresponds to the stated 0.5%; and whether adaptive attacks optimize through the deployed mask.

Presentation quality needs improvement: there are numerous typos and grammatical errors, inconsistent tensor notation, and unclear transitions between the full-response loss, greedy approximation, and first-token triggering loss.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant NLP security problem with a novel internal-representation defense: rather than rewriting prompts or adding external detectors, CachePrune identifies and masks a very small set of context KV-cache dimensions associated with instruction-following behavior.

The method is computationally attractive at deployment time: it preserves the original prompt, requires no additional test-time LLM calls, prunes only about 0.5% of neurons, and is compatible with cached context reuse. The proposed preferential attribution, neuron aggregation, selective thresholding, and trigger-token approximation form a coherent and technically interesting pipeline.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the method’s scale: three instruction-tuned models, SQuAD, HotpotQA, and WildChat, multiple attack-instruction types, prompt-engineering baselines, attack-transfer experiments, code/text transfer, and adaptive GCG-style attacks. CachePrune consistently gives large ASR reductions while largely retaining clean-task F1, ROUGE, BERTScore, and LLM-judge quality.

Ablations are informative. The experiments examine prune ratio, number of calibration samples, trigger length, masking strength, the selective neuron set, and layer-wise neuron distribution. The transfer results in Figure 5 and Table 2 strengthen the claim that the learned mask is not merely memorizing one attack template.

The appendix supplies substantial implementation detail, including attack templates, calibration procedures, metric code, judge prompts, and hyperparameters. Reporting means and standard deviations over multiple trials also improves empirical credibility.
weaknesses: The deployment assumptions should be stated more prominently. CachePrune requires access to internal KV activations and known context boundaries, so it cannot be directly applied to closed API models or unstructured prompts without reliable delimitation. The paper also does not fully establish cross-dataset or cross-domain generalization of a single learned mask.

The DPO-based theoretical motivation is looser than the empirical method. The analysis uses greedy most-probable responses, removes the logarithm, relies on a hypothetical more-immune reference model, and proves only an asymptotic association rather than equivalence between the attribution loss and the DPO objective. This section is useful intuition but should not be interpreted as a strong theoretical guarantee.

The defense is evaluated only on models up to 8B and primarily on reading-comprehension attacks plus one dialogue-summarization setting. Its behavior in agentic, tool-use, retrieval-augmented action, or multi-turn settings remains uncertain. The adaptive evaluation is valuable, but the GCG budget and token length are still limited.

The comparison is concentrated on prompt-formatting baselines. Direct comparison with stronger activation-editing, detection/filtering, or training-based defenses is limited, and the closest neuron-editing methods are mainly discussed rather than empirically benchmarked. Additional details on how ASR is automatically adjudicated and the exact test-set sizes would improve reproducibility.

The method could affect legitimately useful instructions contained in retrieved context and may induce subtle over-refusal or context-underutilization beyond the measured QA metrics. The paper would benefit from a dedicated benign-context evaluation. There are also several typos and notation inconsistencies, and an explicit code/model-artifact release statement is absent.
